title: Object Relationships
summary: How classes connect to each other — association, aggregation, composition, and dependency — and the lifetime rule that decides which one you're looking at.

blocks.markdown:
Classes rarely work alone — they **relate** to each other, and the kind of relationship shapes your design.

- **Association** — two classes just use one another.
- **Aggregation** — one holds the other, but each can live without it.
- **Composition** — one owns the other; the part dies with the whole.
- **Dependency** — one briefly uses another, no lasting link.

The exam favorite: **aggregation vs composition** comes down to one thing — lifetime.

blocks.subTitle: The four relationships at a glance
blocks.markdown:
One table, one mental model.

| Relation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Association | "uses-a" — a peer link |
| Aggregation | "has-a" — shared, independent lifetime |
| Composition | "owns-a" — exclusive, dependent lifetime |
| Dependency | temporary use, no stored link |

**Inheritance** ("is-a") is a fifth relationship, covered on its own page: [inheritance](inheritance).

**Association** is the loosest link: two classes know about each other and interact, but neither owns the other.

- A `Teacher` and a `Student` are associated — each exists fine without the other.
- Can be **one-to-one**, **one-to-many**, or **many-to-many**.
- Can be **unidirectional** (only one side holds a reference) or **bidirectional** (both do).

If all you can say is "these two talk to each other," it's association.

**Aggregation** is a "whole-part" link where the part has an **independent lifetime** — it can outlive the whole, or belong to more than one whole.

- A `Department` has `Professor`s — but if the department shuts down, professors still exist and can join another one.
- The part is usually passed **in** (constructor or setter), not created **by** the whole.
- Signals shared or optional ownership.

**Composition** is a stricter "whole-part" link: the part has a **dependent lifetime** — it's created and destroyed with the whole, and belongs to exactly one owner.

- A `House` is composed of `Room`s — delete the house, the rooms are gone with it.
- The whole usually **creates** the part internally (`new` inside the constructor), not receives it from outside.
- Strongest form of "has-a"; used when the part has no meaning outside its owner.

blocks.subTitle: The lifetime distinction
blocks.markdown:
The single fact that decides which one you're looking at: **can the part outlive the whole?**

| | Aggregation | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Independent | Dependent (dies with owner) |
| Ownership | Shared / optional | Exclusive |
| Example | Department–Professor | House–Room |

Everything else — UML arrows, wording, "has-a" phrasing — is just a symptom of this one rule.

**Dependency** is the weakest relationship: one class briefly uses another — as a method parameter, return value, or local variable — without holding a lasting reference.

- A `Printer` class that takes a `Document` as a method argument depends on it, but doesn't store it as a field.
- No field, no arrows in memory after the call returns.
- Rule of thumb: association **stores** a reference; dependency **borrows** one.

**Inheritance** ("is-a") is a separate axis from the has-a/uses-a family above — it's about **type**, not ownership.

- A `Car` **is-a** `Vehicle` — that's inheritance.
- A `Car` **has-a** `Engine` — that's composition.
- Mixing them up is a classic design smell: don't inherit just to reuse fields; inherit only when the subtype truly **is** the supertype.

Full treatment: [inheritance](inheritance).

Each relationship has its own arrow — useful to recognize on a whiteboard or in a diagram question.

Row 3 'Composition' line with filled/solid diamond at the whole end. Row 4 'Dependency' dashed line with open arrowhead. Row 5 'Inheritance' solid line with hollow triangle arrowhead pointing to parent. Small 2-3 word labels only. >>>

Memory hook: **filled diamond = composition (solid ownership)**, **hollow diamond = aggregation (loose ownership)**.

blocks.subTitle: Composition vs aggregation

blocks.markdown:
Common mix-ups:

- **"Aggregation and composition are the same, just weaker/stronger."** They differ in one concrete thing: who controls the part's lifetime.
- **Confusing dependency with association.** If there's no stored field, it's dependency, not association.
- **Using inheritance for code reuse alone.** If it's not a true is-a, prefer composition — "favor composition over inheritance."

blocks.subTitle: Aggregation vs composition
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between aggregation and composition?**

Both are "has-a" relationships between a whole and its parts. The difference is **lifetime**: in aggregation the part can exist independently and outlive the whole (Department–Professor); in composition the part is created and destroyed with the whole and has no meaning outside it (House–Room).

If you can only remember one line: **composition = solid diamond = dies together; aggregation = hollow diamond = lives apart.**

blocks.subTitle: Association vs dependency
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How is association different from dependency?**

Association is a **lasting** link — one class holds a reference to another as a field, so the relationship persists across calls. Dependency is **temporary** — one class uses another only within a method (as a parameter, return type, or local variable) with nothing stored afterward.

Quick test: does a field exist after the method returns? Yes → association. No → dependency.

blocks.subTitle: Give a composition example
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Give a real-world composition example and explain why it's not aggregation.**

A `Car` and its `Engine`: the engine is built as part of constructing the car and has no independent existence in the system — it's not shared with another car and doesn't outlive this one. Compare to a `Car` and its `Driver`, which is aggregation: the driver exists before and after driving this particular car.

blocks.subTitle: Is-a vs has-a
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you decide between is-a (inheritance) and has-a (composition/aggregation)?**

Ask whether the subtype must satisfy every contract of the supertype — substitutable everywhere it's used. If yes, it's genuinely is-a. If you're only borrowing behavior or fields without that substitutability, model it as has-a instead: give the class a field of that type rather than extending it.

blocks.subTitle: Spotting it in a UML diagram
blocks.markdown:
**Q: You're handed a UML diagram — how do you tell aggregation and composition apart at a glance?**

Look at the diamond at the "whole" end of the line: **hollow/open diamond is aggregation**, **filled/solid diamond is composition**. If there's no diamond at all, it's plain association; a dashed line with an open arrowhead is dependency.
